#65837. Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept.
  • With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.
  • The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

Sources indicate that the GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

NASA's Voyager 1 mission forever changed our view of Jupiter

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone.
  • It has been revealed that while we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune.
  • One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

It has been revealed that while we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Industry observers note that voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Sources indicate that voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which debuted half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

Just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

According to recent reports, this discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation showed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

Taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons showed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency announced its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Industry observers note that voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

#65830. We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1682 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Industry observers note that AI is already powering latest, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar.
  • Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that AI is already powering latest, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?

Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams showed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a newly introduced worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.

In a recent development, the results hint at a new way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, says AI researcher Jonas Guan.

AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he says, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”.

Sources indicate that here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.

In a recent development, historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, indicates Guan, of the University of Toronto.

Recent findings suggest that that adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments showed. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.

According to recent reports, still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.

It has been revealed that and there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.).

Most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan says. But new versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI tech giant Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.

It has been revealed that “The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How promptly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.

Sources indicate that the Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” says cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.

Rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan states.

Guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.

Sources indicate that the octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a newly introduced device, the head would use AI to strategy how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler says. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.

It has been revealed that an attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover new places to copy itself (third image).

In a recent development, J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

In a recent development, J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

The head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan says.).

In a recent development, the octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan says they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.

In a recent development, meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers showed another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan says the company’s work demonstrates that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.

Recent findings suggest that and that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.

Industry observers note that anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that indicated it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.

Whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan says. And AI worms do have weaknesses.

In a recent development, for one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still big programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma states. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.

Ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.

Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler claims.

Recent findings suggest that guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan says. “We are working on the problem day and night.”.

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Many fields of science have struggled under the second Trump administration, with funding cuts and delays plaguing research in fields such as public health and climate science. But some topics have found firmer footing, including artificial intelligence and quantum science.

These technologies, along with supercomputing, “are going to be the three legs of the stool that is going to transform how science and engineering is done,” claims Darío Gil, undersecretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy.

Recent findings suggest that in November 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order to launch the Genesis Mission, a $5 billion whole-of-government effort to advance science via artificial intelligence. The initiative began with the DOE but has since expanded to more than 15 federal agencies.

In a recent development, in June, the president issued an executive order that aims to accelerate the development of tools such as quantum computers, quantum sensors and quantum networks. And in July, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy issued a 123-page report describing its vision for a “golden age” of federal science, in which agencies align investments in research and development with administration priorities.

Federal agencies spent some $4.2 billion on AI R&D in 2025, according to an arm of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy that quantifies such investments.

Many scientists are enthusiastic about the opportunities for AI and quantum research. But some caution that a measured approach is needed. “My strongest opinion … is that I want to see all fields of science supported,” indicates Brad Marston, a physicist at Brown University and president of the American Physical Society. “Priorities have to be chosen, but getting a good balance is important, because you never know where some advance will come from.”.

In a recent development, through Genesis, the DOE looks to use its troves of data as well as experimental and computing facilities to produce a common set of AI tools and a shared ecosystem for science. “That’s conceptually a very powerful idea,” says astronomer Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. “And if it pans out as intended, it could drive great advances in science and technology.”.

Sources indicate that this year, DOE funded nearly 300 projects through Genesis — including one led by Mandelbaum. Her team’s effort aims to unify immense datasets from astronomical facilities around the world, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument and the Zwicky Transient Facility. That would enable AI models to be trained on the data, which could help uncover hidden astronomical insights.

According to recent reports, H. Stockebrand/RubinObs/NOIRLab/AURA/SLAC/DOE/NSF.

Other projects include efforts to accelerate nuclear reactor development, create simulations of the U.S. electric grid and study nuclear fusion. And federal agencies including the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health have rolled out their own Genesis efforts, centered around the mission’s National Science and Technology Challenges, which include topics in health, biology, energy, space, national security and more.

In a recent development, many scientists were already wielding AI in their work. But Genesis “really did create an inflection point,” says John Sarrao, director of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, Calif. SLAC is now involved with 20 Genesis projects and leads two.

Sources indicate that compared with AI, quantum technologies are less mature. With quantum computing, “we’re still at mile one or two or three of a marathon,” says Celia Merzbacher, executive director of the Quantum Economic Development Consortium, a coalition of public and private institutions that works to bolster quantum tech in the United States. Nevertheless, researchers hope the two technologies can amplify one another. AI could help design and develop quantum computers, for example, while quantum computing shows promise for efficiently tackling certain machine learning problems.

Sources indicate that accordingly, several Genesis projects involve quantum error correction, quantum sensors and quantum materials. And the DOE’s Quantum Genesis initiative aims to develop scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computers by 2028.

It has been revealed that AI and quantum were not always hot topics. “Both of those areas … were kind of backwaters until recent advances,” Marston states. Before the development of deep neural networks, for example, AI was mostly a curiosity. “It points to the importance of having a balanced approach to science funding,” he says. What starts as an obscure scientific specialty may suddenly explode into wide relevance.

In the context of limited resources, prioritizing one area of research necessitates deprioritizing another. While some funding for the DOE’s portion of Genesis came from the One Big Beautiful Bill passed in 2025, much of the rest came from the DOE’s budget.

In a recent development, as excited as Mandelbaum is about Genesis, she is concerned about funding for non-AI related work. A cosmology grant her group received from the DOE didn’t align with Genesis mission priorities and was reduced this year, she states. “If the reality is that some of this [funding] is coming out of the baseline research budget in my field, then I think that it would be beneficial for the DOE to engage the scientific community about those trade-offs,” Mandelbaum says.

In response to these concerns, Gil says that the money going to Genesis from the DOE’s Office of Science — about $400 million so far — is small compared to the office’s total FY2026 budget of $8.4 billion.

According to recent reports, sarrao claims that it’s key to build on the momentum of Genesis while still supporting the DOE’s core research. His impression is that things are trending in the right direction. “Are there really exciting opportunities? Yes, 100 percent,” Sarrao says. “Are there risks if you get the balance wrong? Equally well, 100 percent.”.

Industry News: Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept.
  • Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.
  • Sources noted Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who at the moment serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources noted Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who at the moment serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”.

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

Recent findings suggest that the move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Sources indicate that homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Industry observers note that paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”.

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

Recent findings suggest that after Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Recent findings suggest that clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker remarked. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”.

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

According to recent reports, over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Recent findings suggest that collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”.

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

#65822. What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1289 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • For the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a newly introduced set of patients.
  • Sources indicate that kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

For the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a newly introduced set of patients. They show up at the University of Kansas Health System hospital in Kansas City with what looks like severe opiate withdrawal: nausea, vomiting and muscle aches. They’re extremely anxious and sometimes hallucinating. But they haven’t taken an opioid, like fentanyl or heroin. Instead, they’ve used something labeled as kratom, though it may not contain kratom at all.

Sources indicate that kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids. But souped-up fresh versions with hyperpotent derivatives of the active compound are sold online and in gas stations. The derivatives act strongly on the body’s opioid receptors and are often far more powerful than the opioid drugs they are sometimes intended to replace. Kratom products — sold as pills, liquid shots, edibles and more — are often mislabeled, and state and federal regulations lag far behind.

A 2026 survey estimated that about 5 million Americans have used kratom or similar products, and the increased use has sent kratom-related exposures up 1,200 percent from only 258 exposures in 2015, according to the National Poison Data System.

Sources indicate that now, newer versions of the substance can produce withdrawal symptoms like nausea and vomiting, which are often so severe they bring people to the hospital. Here’s what to know.

Sources indicate that kratom comes from the dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa, a tree native to Southeast Asia. Dutch scientist Pieter Willem Korthals first described it in 1839. But “without a doubt, it was used likely for centuries prior to that” in countries including Thailand, Indonesia and Myanmar, claims Oliver Grundmann, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida in Gainesville. “Wherever there is a stream, these trees are growing there.” People chewed the leaves for a stimulant effect and brewed them into a tea to treat pain,” Grundmann says.

According to recent reports, in the United States, kratom is billed pain treatment that is more “natural” than opiates like morphine, Sethi says. “When you take this product at low doses, it is used for waking up … but at higher doses it becomes opiate-like.” Others take it to treat withdrawal or cravings from opioid use.

The leaf form contains more than 40 different naturally occurring chemicals called alkaloids that could have psychoactive effects. The most vital is mitragynine, which makes up two-thirds of the plant’s alkaloid content.

Mitragynine acts on the body’s mu opioid receptors. These receptors — found in the brain, spinal cord and gut — usually respond to natural peptide signals in the body such as endorphins, signaling cells to produce pain relief and release chemicals like dopamine. The receptors get their name from the most famous drug that binds to them: opium. Mitragynine is not derived from or related to opium or morphine but it binds partially to the receptor.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s kind of like a dimmer switch versus turning on the lights,” states Mallory Pullman, a clinical toxicologist at the Mississippi Poison Control Center at the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson. “You don’t fully light your room.”.

Mitragynine also hits receptors that bind norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine receptors, states Grundmann. The activity at adrenergic receptors creates a stimulant-like effect. “Now I think when we look at mitragynine, it’s primarily kind of this duality of the adrenergic and the opioid receptor activity,” he says, producing stimulating and depressive results in turn.

What nature made, chemists and consumers are happy to tweak.

As the kratom leaf is dried, Grundmann says, tiny amounts of mitragynine metabolize into another alkaloid, 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH. After someone takes kratom, the body also converts some mitragynine to 7-OH. The small chemical tweak changes the compound from one that binds partially to the mu opioid receptors to one that binds fully — like morphine or opium, Grundmann says. 7-OH binds 10 times more strongly to mu opioid receptors than mitragynine does. The resulting product is far more potent in its effects and addictive potential.

Sources indicate that when people use the leaves alone, the amount of 7-OH is extremely limited. But by the mid-2010s, scientists found products with more than 500 percent more 7-OH than in the plant alone, and now, consumers can buy products labeled as pure 7-OH.

Industry observers note that while 7-OH can be described as “natural” because it can, in theory, occur in nature, toxicologists like Pullman are also seeing synthetic derivatives that are even stronger, including one molecule named MGM-15. MGM-15 is sold as a “research chemical” and is four times more powerful than 7-OH.

What is in kratom products may not always be what’s on the label, leaving users in the dark about what they are taking. In a 2026 analysis of 44 different kratom products, including tablets, dissolvable films and edibles, Pullman and her colleagues found that 85 percent of the products had contents that did not match the label. Some advertised kratom but contained very high levels of 7-OH. Others had alkaloids that weren’t listed at all.

It’s “very concerning at a consumer level if you can’t trust what’s actually on the label,” Pullman states.

According to recent reports, sethi started hearing the word kratom about 10 years ago in her work with people seeking treatment for opioid use. “I would have patients intermittently tell me about kratom use,” she says. People were using kratom to stay off opioids, or to treat pain, and didn’t report being addicted to the plant.

Now, it’s a different story, Sethi states.

Patients who started using kratom or 7-OH to get off opioids “now are having really bad withdrawal and cravings and ending up in the hospital,” she says. Some are seeking addiction treatment, not for opioids, but for kratom and 7-OH. In 2025, U.S. poison centers documented 3,434 kratom-related exposure reports, reported both by people who called the center and medical professionals. “I see less fentanyl and more kratom at this point, or more 7-OH,” Sethi says.

In July of 2026, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily classified some kratom derivatives as Schedule I drugs, meaning they have high abuse potential and no medical use. Those derivatives include 7-OH and another related kratom derivative, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl or MGPI, as well as MGM-15 and its powerful sibling MGM-16. The DEA re-upped the temporary scheduling of MGM-15 and 16 and MGPI in October. 7-OH was temporarily placed in Schedule I at any dose higher than that found in the kratom plant. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has also issued statements warning consumers not to use the products. None of these measures affect the legality of the kratom leaf itself.

Regulations vary at the state level: Twenty-six states don’t regulate kratom at all, while six states and the District of Columbia list kratom’s ingredients as a Schedule I controlled substance, like the current federal scheduling. A further 18 states regulate sale and manufacture in some way.

“I think there’s a lot more concern now, especially that there might be potential opioids out on the market,” Pullman indicates. Regulations are trying to thread the needle between banning the plant and banning high-potency derivatives, knowing that when one derivative gets smacked down, another will swiftly appear in its place. That cycle is a familiar one, mirroring the evolution and development of synthetic opioids.

Sources indicate that “There’s risk with everything,” she indicates. “I think it’s important to distinguish the difference between a synthetic product versus the natural, and that way we can clearly attribute where the risk lies.”.

  • The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.
  • The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition states.

Recent findings suggest that trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Industry observers note that immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

It has been revealed that the D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a upcoming removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”.

Industry observers note that last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

Recent findings suggest that the case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

Recent findings suggest that the case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

#65816. Breaking: The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1860 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.
  • The highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 17, 2026 at 12:50 pm.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.

The highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17. Analyses of cases dated from when the first outbreak began in 2025 in West Texas through part of 2026 revealed the virus has been spreading uninterrupted for more than a year. That benchmark signals measles is no longer under control.

Industry observers note that the United States is not alone. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status, PAHO revealed; Canada had lost it in 2025. “Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage,” PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa remarked in a Nov. 17 news conference. “And this global trend is also affecting the Americas.” Countries will need to not only stop ongoing outbreaks, but also prove that no one caught measles within their borders for a full year to regain measles-free status.

That won’t happen overnight. But there is a way, experts say. Vaccinating people across the country, particularly in areas with low vaccination rates, will stifle the virus’s spread. But so far, the U.S. federal public health response has taken a back seat to efforts from state and local health departments to curb ongoing outbreaks.

Measles’s return “is an enormous black eye on the reputation of the United States,” said epidemiologist Jennifer Nuzzo of the Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I., in a Nov. 9 webinar hosted by the university. The Americas led the global campaign to control the virus, and in 2016 the region became the first to eliminate measles transmission from all its countries.

“To lose [elimination status] means we’re going backwards… meaning decades of progress lost,” Nuzzo said. “It’s an indicator of our lack of protection. It is an indicator of our lack of preparedness for disease threats in general.”.

Industry observers note that PAHO’s verdict comes amid a surge of measles not seen in the United States since 1991. Health officials have recorded more than 7,000 cases since the beginning of the West Texas outbreak. That tally includes nearly 2,300 measles cases in 2025 and 5,412 in 2026 as of November 12, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over 90 percent of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated or whose status is unknown. States report that 13 people have died, although the CDC so far recognizes only nine of those deaths.

While mild measles symptoms include high fever, cough and a rash, roughly 1 in 5 people will be hospitalized with complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Children younger than 5 years and adults over 20 are more likely to get sick, as are pregnant women and their infants. At least 13 babies were born infected, called congenital measles, since the beginning of 2025, researchers report November 16 in NEJM Evidence. Those babies are at risk for developing dangerous brain swelling that is almost always fatal later on in life.

Sources indicate that the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine helped eliminate measles from the United States in 2000. After that, cases still sometimes popped up. Those cases were mostly in unvaccinated people traveling from parts of the world where the virus still widely circulates. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

Industry observers note that but widespread misinformation, including a disproven claim that the vaccine causes autism, means fewer children are receiving the MMR shot and more people are questioning its safety. According to the CDC, roughly 92 percent of kindergarteners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019. And in 2025, 83 percent of U.S. adults viewed the MMR vaccine as safe, down from 86 percent in 2024, according to a survey from the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. Yet decades of evidence show the vaccine is safe and highly effective.

That measles made a comeback is not a surprise, states Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University School of Medicine. Until recently, outbreaks were largely isolated to communities with low vaccination rates and quickly contained. But now, outbreaks seem to be more likely to spill over into neighboring communities, Lo says. “There’s a lot of potential connectedness between the outbreaks.”.

What’s more, some infected people aren’t getting tested, making them invisible to officials who are now struggling to trace chains of transmission. An outbreak that hit Arizona and Utah, for instance, was far larger than official numbers suggest, researchers reported July 15 in a preprint at medRxiv.org. The roughly 1,000 confirmed cases may represent just 20 to 30 percent of the outbreak’s true size.

A functional surveillance system is crucial to keeping outbreaks under control, Jonathan Temte, a family medicine physician at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, said in the Brown University webinar. Without good surveillance across the entire country, “we can miss pockets out there if people aren’t reporting, if people are hiding cases.”.

Industry observers note that but surveillance alone won’t stop the virus from “popcorning across the country,” Nuzzo remarked. “Measles has returned, and it’s going to take vaccination to stop it.”.

Over the last two years, measles outbreaks have popped up across the United States, sickening thousands of people since mid-January 2025. Most of those cases, shown by county where they were reported, are in people who are unvaccinated. Colors on the map indicate the relative number of cases reported. Green represents the lowest and red the highest number of cases. Notable outbreaks have appeared in Utah, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

Michael Mitchell and Andrea Uhlig/Brown University School of Public Health.

Efforts to boost vaccine uptake could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles, but not all. “Figuring out which ones are [high risk] can be a little tricky,” Lo says. “But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”.

According to recent reports, homing in on school districts or individual schools could also help. State health departments typically report vaccination rates among school-age children by county. But that broad metric can hide high risk schools with low vaccination rates, epidemiologists Siyu Chen and Ana Bento reported in August in Nature Medicine. Computer simulations relying on data that included 50,000 schools across the United States showed that school-level estimates best revealed where the virus could gain a foothold. That was true even if county-level vaccination rates were close to 95 percent.

Another element that influenced where measles took off was whether communities with cases were near other areas with low vaccination rates, the team found. The outbreak in Texas, for instance, may have ended faster because communities with low vaccination rates were farther away from one another compared with outbreaks in South Carolina and Pennsylvania, claims Bento, of Cornell University. Neighboring areas where many are unvaccinated may face longer-burning outbreaks. “Which is what we are now seeing,” Bento says.

It has been revealed that measles elimination status can be regained. The declaration that the virus is endemic is “not a punishment,” Bento says. It’s a sign that something needs to change. That might include vaccine catch-up campaigns, community outreach or getting rid of nonmedical vaccine exemptions.

According to recent reports, local public health officials are “doing every last thing that you can imagine with limited resources,” health psychologist Noel T. Brewer mentioned in a Nov. 12 webinar hosted by the Association of Health Care Journalists. But a cohesive blueprint at the federal level could bolster defenses before the virus arrives in new states, noted Brewer, of the University of North Carolina Gillings School of Global Public Health in Chapel Hill.

Sources indicate that such efforts could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles. “A subset [with low vaccination rates] are high risk,” Lo says. “Figuring out which ones are which can be a little tricky. But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”.

There’s also wiggle room in the childhood vaccine schedule to provide kids extra protection. Normally children don’t get their first MMR dose until their first birthday. But doctors can give infants an extra MMR dose at 6 months if there is an active outbreak in their area. Pediatricians can also offer the second dose a month after the first one, rather than waiting until around the time children start kindergarten. Adults, particularly those who received only one dose, can also get a booster. It’s unclear whether health officials will officially recommend such actions.

“The problem is that there’s no trusted source for this vaccine decision anymore,” Lo says. Previous vaccine recommendations were up to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which was disbanded in March after lawsuits blocked appointments made by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Now, there’s a lot of different medical societies and initiatives to try and fill that void,” Lo says. But it’s unclear which would be best positioned to lead.

It has been revealed that CDC director Erica Schwartz has noted the health agency will not be changing its response to ongoing outbreaks. “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” she told Reuters. The CDC did not respond to Science News requests for an interview, but shared in a Nov. 17 statement that the agency will “encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”.

Recent findings suggest that eliminating measles again will take dedicated resources and more funding funneled to public health departments across the country, Lo notes. “You see increasing measles outbreaks and a lot of time and resources to contain these outbreaks at a time where you’re slashing budgets,” Lo says, “that’s a really bad mismatch.”.

Sources indicate that public health responses to measles are expensive. Officials in Upcoming Mexico spent an estimated $5.4 million — over $53,000 per case — responding to a 2025 outbreak that was linked to West Texas. The CDC has provided an additional $100 million to states to help fight measles.

Other countries have beaten back measles after an unwelcome return. Extensive vaccination campaigns helped Venezuela and Brazil regain measles elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019. The Public Health Agency of Canada also revealed that its nearly two-year-long outbreak officially ended in October, though it’s unclear when the country might earn its status back.

“It is not hopeless,” Nuzzo said. “It can be done, and I hope it will be done [in the United States].”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

According to recent reports, colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

In a recent development, running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

Sources indicate that this year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

#65809. Cracks in public health grew in 2026
