#65793. Industry News: Fatal cases of Ebola often share a striking pattern

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1458 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Fatal cases of Ebola often share a striking pattern

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1458 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ebola may trap immune messages inside infected cells, keeping the body's defenses active longer and potentially worsening illness.
  • A deadly virus such as Ebola might be expected to kill by shutting down the body’s defenses.
  • Ebola virus does make proteins that block a key signal the body uses to fight infection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ebola may trap immune messages inside infected cells, keeping the body's defenses active longer and potentially worsening illness.

A deadly virus such as Ebola might be expected to kill by shutting down the body’s defenses.

Ebola virus does make proteins that block a key signal the body uses to fight infection. The pattern in patients, however, is the opposite.

People who die from Ebola often show the highest activity in the genes that fight viruses.

Scientists have struggled to explain this for years.

In a recent development, A upcoming study points to the tiny droplets of protein and RNA that Ebola virus builds inside infected cells. These droplets are known as viral condensates, and the cell’s own immune messages become trapped inside them.

Once trapped, the messages are not broken down when they should be.

The defense therefore remains switched on. That prolonged response may be part of what makes patients so ill.

The findings come during a major outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

As of November 17, the CDC reported 11,613 confirmed cases and 5,678 confirmed deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The outbreak involves Bundibugyo virus, a close relative of the virus studied here.

Seven genes is all Ebola virus carries.

In a recent development, two of them make proteins called NP and VP35. Both attach to viral RNA and to each other, gathering into droplets that have no outer membrane.

During an infection they can take up between one-fifth and one-third of a cell.

Jingru Fang led the work in the Saphire Lab at the La Jolla Institute for Immunology. Fang now works at Princeton University’s Omenn-Darling Bioengineering Institute.

“When birds land in a newly introduced place, they make nests where they can raise their babies,” said Fang.

“You can imagine viral condensates as nests for a virus.”.

To study the droplets, NP and VP35 were introduced into human kidney cells. The actual virus was left out, and the droplets still formed.

According to recent reports, the messenger RNA in those cells was then stained. Messenger RNA carries the instructions a cell uses to make a protein.

Messenger RNA was more concentrated inside the droplets than in the surrounding cell fluid.

In human cells, the buildup came to roughly 40%. Kidney cells from Egyptian fruit bats indicated an even greater buildup.

When NP was changed so that it could no longer attach to single-stranded RNA, that buildup fell by about half.

A similar change to VP35 had little effect in human cells. NP appears to play the bigger role in collecting RNA.

That figure covers every message at once, and states nothing about which ones are collected.

The team therefore used a method capable of reading thousands of RNA types at once, across 136 genes linked to Ebola infection and the immune response.

Recent findings suggest that about 90,000 cells were examined, with droplets found in roughly 30% of them. Of the 66 genes measured reliably, all but two were more concentrated inside.

In a recent development, the amount of RNA made little difference. Rare messages collected inside while far more common ones stayed out, indicating that something other than abundance determined where they ended up.

Shape proved to be the better explanation.

RNA is not always a straight strand. Parts of it join together wherever the letters match, folding the molecule into loops and stems.

Messages with fewer folds in their protein-making sections entered more readily.

In a recent development, to test this, the genetic instructions in some messages were rewritten. The fresh versions made the same protein but folded differently, and those with fewer folds entered more readily.

In a recent development, ten viruses that carry negative-strand RNA were also examined, including Ebola, measles, rabies and Marburg. In all of them the protein-making regions had fewer folds than the human messages left outside.

Recent findings suggest that the most striking finding concerned interferon. Type I interferon, released when a cell detects a virus, switches on hundreds of defense genes in nearby cells.

After the cells were treated with interferon, the droplets started collecting different messages.

Messages from more than 20 defense genes appeared in droplets.

It has been revealed that the rule governing entry also changed. The protein-making section was no longer the best indicator.

Instead the tail of each message mattered more, the stretch that follows the instructions for making a protein.

Immune defense messages often have long, tightly folded tails.

The more folded the tail, the more of that message was found inside. Interferon also increases proteins that attach to RNA, and some of these may help pull immune messages into the droplets.

According to recent reports, people who die from Ebola often show stronger activity in their defense genes than those who survive. Even people who recover can show signs of inflammation-related gene activity years later.

Erica Ollmann Saphire, who led the study with Fang, is the president and chief executive of the La Jolla Institute for Immunology.

“These are strong immune responses, but they’re not working well,” noted Ollmann Saphire.

It has been revealed that cells normally break down messenger RNA once it has served its purpose. Enzymes such as XRN1 help carry out that cleanup.

Staining demonstrated less XRN1 inside the droplets than in the surrounding cell fluid.

This raised a further question: whether messages trapped inside survive longer because the enzymes cannot reach them.

It has been revealed that messages held in the droplets broke down more slowly than the same messages in cells carrying a modified NP that could not bind RNA. Messages that stayed outside broke down at similar rates in both groups.

“The antiviral response is like a weapon, and cells use degradation as a way to deactivate that weapon,” Fang explained.

Protein production also changed. A protein the cell requires in order to start building other proteins was largely missing from the droplets.

Without interferon, more messenger RNA collected inside but less protein came out of it.

With interferon, both rose: one defense message increased more than sixfold, and levels of two defense proteins rose alongside it.

A final experiment used a weakened Ebola virus, one lacking a gene needed for replication.

A defense message called IFIT3 was found inside the droplets of those infected cells as well.

Bats can carry filoviruses without getting sick. These viruses belong to the same family as Ebola.

Bat genes cannot be read with tools designed for human RNA. Computer models were therefore used to predict how 45 of the collected messages would fold, in bats, ferrets and macaques.

Ferrets and macaques can become seriously ill from Ebola, which makes them useful comparisons.

Within the defense genes, the bat versions had tails that were less tightly folded than the human ones. Ferret and macaque tails were much more like those in humans.

Genes outside the defense group revealed no meaningful difference between species.

Fever often comes with an interferon response, so the predictions were repeated at 102 degrees Fahrenheit (39 degrees Celsius).

Messages carrying bat tails then behaved as the folding had predicted. The least folded bat tail kept its message out of the droplets better than the matching human tail.

Industry observers note that bat immune messages may therefore be less likely to become trapped. If they remain outside, cells can break them down at the usual time.

Most experiments used kidney cells grown in a laboratory. The process was not tested in human patients or living animals, and for much of the work NP and VP35 stood in for the complete virus.

The cells were measured at just one point, 24 hours after the proteins were introduced, across 136 genes out of roughly 20,000.

The human kidney cells responded poorly to interferon. Higher concentrations were therefore used for longer periods than other tissues might need.

It has been revealed that the RNA folding patterns were computer predictions. They cannot fully show how every RNA molecule behaves inside a living cell.

Sources indicate that the bat comparison included only one species. It was chosen partly because scientists have not yet identified Ebola virus’s natural host.

“We don’t know whether this difference can explain everything, but it gives researchers a place to start looking and confirm what we’ve found in additional human or animal samples,” Fang added.

It has been revealed that breaking the droplets apart may be worth pursuing as a treatment, the authors wrote. It could slow the virus and prevent immune messages from remaining active too long.

The principal challenge is achieving that inside living cells without destroying the cells.

The full study was published in the journal Cell.

#65792. Even slightly warmer summers are linked to a higher death risk for people with heart disease

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1428 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Even slightly warmer summers are linked to a higher death risk for people with heart disease

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1428 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A UK study links extreme heat and repeated heatwaves to higher death risks among people with heart disease.
  • An average summer temperature of about 62°F (16.5°C) sounds mild.
  • In a large UK study, researchers found that for every 1.8°F (1°C) increase in average summer temperature, patients had a 15% higher risk of dying from any cause.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A UK study links extreme heat and repeated heatwaves to higher death risks among people with heart disease.

An average summer temperature of about 62°F (16.5°C) sounds mild. But even slightly warmer summers were linked to a higher risk of death among people with cardiovascular disease.

In a large UK study, researchers found that for every 1.8°F (1°C) increase in average summer temperature, patients had a 15% higher risk of dying from any cause.

The risk was also higher among patients who experienced more heat waves. The odds of death rose on the hottest days and after sharp jumps in temperature from one day to the next.

Industry observers note that taken together, the findings indicate that heat may influence survival across entire seasons in heart patients. An influence during brief hot spells is suggested as well.

Sources indicate that the research was conducted by Ka Yan Lai of the University of Hong Kong alongside colleagues there. Further collaborators were based at the University of Oxford.

Using health records, the investigators followed nearly 64,000 UK patients for periods of up to 16 years.

Lai said the health effects of extreme heat have “rarely been studied among people with pre-existing conditions.”.

Industry observers note that all of the patients had been enrolled in UK Biobank, a long-running British health project. Half a million volunteers aged between 37 and 73 were recruited to it from 2006 to 2010.

From this pool, 63,860 volunteers were selected by the team for analysis.

All received their first hospital diagnosis of cardiovascular disease between 2006 and 2022.

Cardiovascular disease, or CVD, includes conditions that affect the heart and blood vessels.

Four of those disorders were examined on their own as well. Atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat, was the first of them.

In a recent development, the second was ischemic heart disease, in which narrowed arteries can’t deliver enough blood to the heart. Heart failure and stroke made up the remaining two.

It has been revealed that at diagnosis, the patients had reached an average age of about 69 years. Deaths from any cause had been recorded for 12,237 of them by the end of 2022.

That figure corresponds to roughly one patient in five.

In a recent development, temperature data were taken from the daily records kept by the Met Office. Those records are mapped onto squares measuring about 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) across.

For every summer, defined as June through August, each home address was matched to its square.

Considerable variation in average summer temperature was evident across that map. The coldest squares averaged about 43°F (6.1°C), whereas the warmest reached about 66°F (18.7°C).

Recent findings suggest that the central result relates to the average summer temperature at each patient’s place of residence. A 15% higher risk of death was associated with every additional 1.8°F (1°C).

In a recent development, several other influences had been accounted for before that estimate was produced. Among them were age, sex, smoking, alcohol use, diabetes and neighborhood deprivation.

For patients with ischemic heart disease, each added degree Celsius corresponded to a 19% higher risk. A smaller increase of 10% was found among those with atrial fibrillation.

The results for heart failure and stroke were less certain. In both groups, the link with average summer temperature was too weak to exclude chance.

Adults aged 65 and older in New England had been examined in an earlier US study.

A 1% increase in deaths was reported there for each 1.8°F (1°C) rise in long-term average summer temperature. Older adults in general were covered by that work, not only people with heart disease.

It has been revealed that heat waves were also counted by the researchers. A heat wave was defined as two or more consecutive days hotter than 90% of local summer days.

According to recent reports, exposure to four or more heat waves a year was experienced by some patients. Their risk of death exceeded by 24% that of patients exposed to two or fewer.

Among patients with atrial fibrillation, the corresponding increase in risk was 29%. It stood at 28% among those with heart failure.

A second analysis was restricted to patients whose deaths occurred during a summer.

For each such patient, temperatures on the day of death and the five preceding days were examined. These were then compared with other days in the same month that fell on the same weekday.

It has been revealed that because every patient served as their own comparison, fixed traits can’t account for the results. Sex and schooling are examples of such traits.

On the hottest 1% of summer days, the odds of death among the patients as a group were 70% higher. The reference point was the temperature at which deaths were lowest.

Temperature changes from one day to the next were measured as well. The largest one-day rises were taken to be those in the top 1% of such changes.

After rises of that size, the odds of death were roughly double those seen when temperature held constant.

Roughly threefold odds were found in patients with ischemic heart disease or heart failure.

Industry observers note that considerable uncertainty surrounds the estimates for sharp rises. In heart failure, the plausible range extended from 36% higher odds to more than seven times as high.

No clear link with deaths was detected for sudden drops in temperature.

Events inside the patients’ bodies were not measured at any point in the study. A plausible explanation was instead drawn by the authors from earlier research on extreme heat.

Sources indicate that in hot weather, warm blood is pumped toward the skin so that heat can be shed by the body. As much as 5 gallons (20 liters) of blood may be pumped by the heart each minute.

Sweating can meanwhile strip water and salt from the body. Blood that holds less water becomes thicker, and thicker blood may clot more readily.

In a person with heart disease, the extra pumping may require more oxygen than the heart can obtain.

Among patients lacking a college or university degree, warmer summers were tied more strongly to death. A weaker link was seen in patients who held such a degree.

A similar contrast emerged between neighborhoods with moderate green space and the greenest neighborhoods, where the link was weaker.

Among heart failure patients, the link was stronger in the most deprived neighborhoods.

Several possible reasons were put forward by the authors. Deprived neighborhoods tend to be overcrowded and to suffer more air pollution and traffic noise, they wrote.

Physically demanding work in extreme weather is also more common among people with less money.

Green spaces, meanwhile, have been shown in earlier studies to cool their surroundings.

Recent findings suggest that according to Lai, protection will have to be delivered at several levels at once. City planning was named as one of those levels.

Sources indicate that cooling strategies form another, as do personal decisions about where to live. Lai said such protection is needed most by the most vulnerable groups.

Extreme heat is projected to grow more frequent and more intense as populations age. That observation came from study co-author Chinmoy Sarkar of the University of Hong Kong.

Together, he said, those trends will make protecting frail people with chronic diseases a top public health priority.

A link between heat and death can be demonstrated by a study of this kind. Proof that heat caused the deaths lies beyond its reach.

Because temperatures were assigned by home address, the patients’ actual whereabouts each day remain unrecorded. Nor was any information available on air-conditioning use or on changes in medication.

Smoking and drinking habits were recorded only once, when volunteers joined UK Biobank.

Those habits may well have changed afterward. Since cases were identified through hospital admissions, milder disease that never led to admission was missed.

Recent findings suggest that UK Biobank volunteers may also differ from the wider population. About 96% of the patients in this study were white. The authors wrote that the volunteers may not represent everyone in the UK with cardiovascular disease.

Industry observers note that none of the patients was given a cooler home or a greener street during the study. How many deaths such changes might prevent therefore can’t be read from the records.

Air-conditioning use could be accounted for in future research, as could travel to places with different temperatures.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Climate.

#65790. Ice baths after exercise: What happens when you make them a habit?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (754 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Ice baths after exercise: What happens when you make them a habit?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ice baths may ease soreness after a hard workout, but regular cold plunges after lifting may limit gains in muscle size and strength.
  • An ice bath after a hard workout may ease muscle soreness.
  • A major review led by Edith Cowan University (ECU) found it can blunt long-term strength and muscle gains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ice baths may ease soreness after a hard workout, but regular cold plunges after lifting may limit gains in muscle size and strength.

An ice bath after a hard workout may ease muscle soreness. But taking one after every lifting session may make it harder to build muscle and strength over time.

A major review led by Edith Cowan University (ECU) found it can blunt long-term strength and muscle gains.

According to recent reports, researchers analyzed 15 published systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Together they covered 161 studies and more than 3,200 participants.

In a recent development, the takeaway is simple. Athletes, coaches, and fitness fans should be strategic, not habitual, with ice baths.

“Cold-water immersion is not a one-size-fits-all recovery tool,” said lead author Erfan Berjisian, a PhD student at ECU.

“Its benefits depend heavily on the athlete’s goals, the type of exercise completed, and when the next performance session is scheduled.”.

The review found ice baths are particularly good at reducing muscle soreness. They also lower markers of muscle damage and they help athletes feel recovered faster.

Muscle soreness dropped consistently for up to four days after exercise. Markers of muscle damage were lower between 24 and 72 hours after an ice bath.

Industry observers note that the review also noted a boost in heart rate variability right after exercise. That’s a sign the body is starting to recover.

For athletes who need to compete again soon, the benefits depend on what they’ll be doing and how much time they have to recover.

“Cold-water immersion appears especially useful when recovery time is limited, such as during tournaments, congested competition schedules or repeated high-intensity training sessions,” Berjisian said.

Sources indicate that researchers found endurance performance improved within the first hour after an ice bath. Power and jump performance often improved 24 to 72 hours later.

However, explosive performance actually dropped in the hours right after an ice bath.

That likely happens due to the temporary cooling effect on muscles.

“If athletes need to perform high-speed or explosive movements soon after cooling, cold-water immersion may be counterproductive unless sufficient re-warming occurs,” noted co-author Kristina Kendall from ECU.

Perhaps the most significant finding was about repeated use.

Athletes who constantly used cold-water immersion after resistance training saw smaller improvements in strength, muscle size, and power.

The evidence suggests chronic use may blunt some of the body’s normal muscle-building responses to training.

It has been revealed that the review also found a detail worth noting. The effect on strength may depend on the protocol.

Immersing just the exercised limb was linked to reduced gains. Whole-body immersion showed no clear detrimental effect.

For endurance athletes, it  was a different story. The review found no evidence that regular cold-water immersion harmed aerobic fitness or endurance adaptations.

The results suggest that cold-water immersion at 50–59°F (10–15°C) for 10–15 minutes generally helped with post-workout recovery.

Colder water, at 41–50°F (5–10°C) for the same duration, may help restore jumping performance and lower markers of muscle damage.

Both intermittent and continuous protocols worked, with no clear winner between them.

Sources indicate that the authors also assessed the quality of that evidence. They rated it low to very low.

Most of the samples were male, which limits how well the findings apply to women.

Industry observers note that the authors also flagged some overlap between the reviews, especially the ones on strength and muscle growth. Those conclusions rest on a fairly concentrated group of trials.

In a recent development, the review calls for more work on women and on different training types. It also wants research that tracks athletes over longer periods.

Ice baths may ease soreness when athletes have limited time to recover, and their effects on performance vary with the activity and the timing.

But the science notes athletes should stop treating them as a cure-all.

They should be more cautious when the goal is building strength and muscle mass.

Industry observers note that when races or matches are only a day or two apart, an ice bath may ease soreness before the next event. That can matter during a tournament, when athletes have little time to recover between rounds.

If your goal is to build muscle or get stronger, consider saving the cold plunge for competition days.

Making it a routine after lifting may limit the gains you’re training for.

The study is published in the journal Sports Medicine – Open.

#65786. Industry News: Male bumblebees usually leave the nest, so what happens when they stay?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1189 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Male bumblebees usually leave the nest, so what happens when they stay?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lab experiments found that male bumblebees use their body heat to warm developing young, a task usually associated with queens and workers.
  • In a bumblebee nest, nearly all of the work has long been credited to the females.
  • According to recent reports, the queen founds the colony and her daughters raise the young.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lab experiments found that male bumblebees use their body heat to warm developing young, a task usually associated with queens and workers.

In a bumblebee nest, nearly all of the work has long been credited to the females.

According to recent reports, the queen founds the colony and her daughters raise the young. Males are expected to leave soon after reaching adulthood, mate and then die.

A new study of lab-reared common eastern bumblebees has now found males helping with the young. The developing brood was warmed by the males with their own body heat.

It has been revealed that queens housed with males laid eggs sooner. After 28 days, nests with five males contained about 49 eggs, larvae and pupae on average, compared with 33 in nests with a queen alone.

Sources indicate that the experiments were run by Meghan Moore and Hollis Woodard at the University of California, Riverside. Both are entomologists. Their nests were not natural ones.

Queens were housed with as many as five males and no workers, a mix rarely seen in the wild.

According to recent reports, the project began with photos taken for a different experiment. Moore had pointed a thermal camera at the nests. Bright white patches of heat revealed up on the males.

Bumblebees raise their eggs, larvae and pupae together in a single clump. Biologists call these young the brood. A queen keeps the brood warm much as a hen warms her eggs.

She straddles the clump and presses her abdomen against it. The heat is produced by muscles in her thorax, the middle part of her body.

This posture was first described in 1972 for another bumblebee species.

It has been revealed that on each of 12 days, every nest was photographed four times within one hour. In total, 2,304 usable thermal images were collected.

The images were labeled so that scorers could not tell which kind of nest each one indicated.

It has been revealed that males in the queen’s posture turned out to be hot. Their thoraxes averaged 94.6°F (34.8°C). Males standing on the brood without that posture averaged about 88°F (31°C).

Recent findings suggest that queens in the same posture averaged about 99°F (37.2°C). The males were not simply resting on a warm spot. Heat was being made in their bodies the way a queen makes it, only less of it.

According to recent reports, heat generated in the thorax is passed back to the abdomen. That rear section is the part a bee presses against the brood. Here, too, queens and males behaved differently.

Recent findings suggest that in incubating queens, the abdomen was about 2.9°F (1.6°C) cooler than the thorax. In incubating males, the abdomen was 6.7°F (3.7°C) cooler. Their gap was more than twice as wide.

Sources indicate that A possible reason was offered by the authors, who described it as speculation. Heat is known to damage sperm, including in males of another bumblebee species.

By limiting the heat that reaches his abdomen, a male may protect his sperm.

It has been revealed that no sperm were examined in this study. For now the idea remains untested.

Industry observers note that moore and Woodard began the nest experiment with 75 mated queens. Each queen had been treated with carbon dioxide. This let her skip winter dormancy and begin laying eggs.

Some queens were given a nest box to themselves. Others shared a box with one, three or five young males from other colonies.

Queens living alone needed about 15 days to lay their first eggs. With one male, the wait dropped to about 11 days. It fell to about eight days with three males and about six with five.

A queen with five males therefore started laying in less than half the time of a lone queen.

Industry observers note that every nest was then allowed 28 days to grow, counted from its first eggs. An earlier start on egg laying could not explain a bigger nest at the end.

Recent findings suggest that fifteen queens died before the experiment was over. The brood counts come from the nests that remained.

After those 28 days, nests of lone queens held about 33 eggs, larvae and pupae on average.

Nests with five males held about 49. That is roughly 1.5 times as many. Nests with one or three males fell in between.

Industry observers note that only the nests with five males produced more adult workers during that time. They averaged about five workers per nest. The other groups averaged two or three.

Queens were photographed incubating about as often whether or not males were present.

The photos also showed fewer instances in which no bee was incubating the brood when males were present.

Incubation helps maintain nest temperatures, which in turn support the brood’s development. Where males were photographed incubating more often, more older brood was found at the end.

According to the authors, male incubation may directly support the growth of the brood. They also wrote that more work is needed to show cause.

Nests holding males but no workers are unusual. For that reason a smaller test was also run. Five nests containing both males and worker bees were filmed for 24 hours in darkness with infrared cameras.

Males incubated in all five nests. Two of the nests were young, with fewer than 15 bees. Two others were mature, with 50 or more.

Industry observers note that on video, a male can be picked out by a patch of facial hair. It is sometimes described as a moustache.

Male incubation is not a latest observation.

In 1985, entomologist Sydney Cameron reported that males of a different bumblebee species incubate pupae. Moore and Woodard have now added a second species.

They also measured how nests developed when males were present.

How often males do any of this in wild nests cannot yet be said. Young wild nests usually hold a queen and her workers. Males mostly appear late in the season.

Sources indicate that the lab males were also unable to leave. Any male inclined to fly off had no way to do so. The authors wrote that this may have made the males more likely to incubate.

The bees came from commercially reared colonies, which may behave differently from wild ones. They were also given food instead of foraging for it.

Recent findings suggest that wild bumblebee nests are hard to find. As a result, data on wild colonies that produce males early are scarce.

In a recent development, incubation takes a great deal of energy. What that work costs a male, in energy or in fertility, was not measured.

“What’s the trade-off? There’s no free lunch,” Woodard said.

In a recent development, further studies are planned on whether caring for brood affects the males’ bodies. Future research will also need to test whether male incubation itself makes nests grow. Its importance in wild colonies is still unknown.

The full study was published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

#65785. What makes artwork memorable? Artists put their instincts to the test

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1173 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

What makes artwork memorable? Artists put their instincts to the test

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artists found that making forgettable artwork was harder than making memorable pieces, while AI predicted viewers' memories better.
  • Could you make a painting that someone would look at and forget minutes later?
  • In an art contest, researchers gave artists a choice: Create something viewers would remember or something they would rapidly forget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artists found that making forgettable artwork was harder than making memorable pieces, while AI predicted viewers' memories better.

Could you make a painting that someone would look at and forget minutes later?

In an art contest, researchers gave artists a choice: Create something viewers would remember or something they would rapidly forget.

In a recognition test, entries meant to be memorable were recognized more often than entries meant to be forgettable.

The memorable entries also came closer to the researchers’ target for their category.

A computer model called ResMem, trained on photographs, was better than artists and a separate group of raters at sorting the most- and least-remembered artworks.

Trent Davis and Yifei Chen carried out the study together with Wilma Bainbridge of the University of Chicago.

Bainbridge leads the Brain Bridge Lab there and is an associate professor in the Department of Psychology.

Memory was tested within minutes of the art having been seen in every part of the study.

For three months the art contest remained open to adult artists who lived in the continental United States.

Each of them was permitted to enter a single piece and had to choose a category for it. Memorable and forgettable were the two categories on offer and an artist could not enter both.

Industry observers note that the organizers accepted only flat physical works, of which paintings, drawings, and collages are examples. Digital art and photography had been excluded under the rules that the team had drawn up.

Recent findings suggest that in all, 144 submissions were received from 20 states and 86 of them met the rules. Of those 86 artworks, 62 had been entered as memorable and the other 24 as forgettable.

The first memory test was completed online by a group of 119 adults who were living in the United States. All 86 of the artworks were presented to these viewers one after another in a single long stream.

Some of the artworks were shown for a second time once at least 30 seconds had passed. The viewers had been instructed to press a key whenever they believed that an artwork had appeared before.

A score for every artwork in the contest was then worked out by the team from those key presses.

Mean scores of 0.86 and 0.79 out of 1 were obtained for memorable and forgettable entries respectively. Although modest in size, this difference was unlikely to be attributable to chance.

A high target score had been set by the team for memorable entries and a low one for forgettable entries.

It was found that the memorable entries had come closer to their target than the forgettable entries had.

The team then selected the works that had been remembered best and worst by the online viewers.

Thirty-nine of those works were shown for a month at Connect Gallery in the Hyde Park neighborhood of Chicago.

In a recent development, sixty-two visitors walked through the show and were free to look at the works in whatever order they wished. They had been informed that memory was the theme of the show but not that a test would follow.

Recognition was assessed afterward in a separate room where artworks were presented to the visitors on their own phones.

A mean of 89% of the tested visitors recognized any given piece from the best-remembered group. The corresponding proportion for pieces from the least-remembered group was 70% of the visitors.

Industry observers note that bainbridge called the show a risky experiment for the lab. Visitors to a small exhibition about memory had been given a reason to try to remember each of the pieces.

Works from the two groups had for the most part been hung on opposite walls of the gallery.

The test was therefore repeated with 141 people at a vision science conference where paper prints were mixed together.

The works remembered best online were again recognized more often than the works that had been remembered least.

According to recent reports, the artworks were also rated on 21 qualities by a separate group of 892 people. One of those qualities was the degree to which each artwork seemed memorable to the person rating it.

The works described as memorable by these raters were not reliably the ones remembered by online viewers. It was the goals chosen by the artists that the ratings were instead found to match.

Higher memorability ratings were given to art that people found complex, surprising, interesting, or likely to become famous.

The works that viewers tended to remember were those that raters felt able to rebuild easily in the mind. Works in which a person was shown were also remembered better whereas landscapes were remembered worse.

Works that looked digitally made were remembered better too. Every entry in the contest had nevertheless been made by hand.

“What people think is memorable is different from what actually is,” Chen said.

ResMem is a neural network, which is a kind of AI program that learns from examples. It was built in Bainbridge’s lab and was trained on nearly 70,000 photographs.

The model takes in an image and returns a score that highlights how likely people are to remember it.

In an earlier study, memory for more than 4,000 paintings from the Art Institute of Chicago was predicted by ResMem.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers compared three ways of predicting which artworks people would remember. They looked at the 20 most remembered and the 20 least remembered pieces.

The AI model, ResMem, correctly sorted 80% of the 40 artworks. The artists’ own choices were correct 67.5% of the time.

The separate group’s ratings correctly classified 62.5% of the artworks.

According to recent reports, resMem also predicted which artworks gallery visitors would remember. People’s ratings could not do this reliably.

The researchers think the AI model may perform better because it does not judge art the way people do. For example, people may assume that interesting or surprising art is easier to remember, even when that is not true.

The study did not explain why making memorable art was easier than making forgettable art.

It has been revealed that researchers think memorable images may share certain features that catch people’s attention. Forgettable images may not have anything in common, making them harder to create on purpose.

Artists chose whether to enter the contest and which category to compete in. Some had taught themselves to make art, while others had master’s degrees in fine arts.

Neither education nor professional experience clearly affected their success. However, the researchers had only basic information about their training.

Gallery visitors may also have been more interested in art than the people who took the online test.

The researchers want to study more highly trained artists. They also suggest tracking where people look in a gallery to better understand which artworks stay in their memory.

The full study was published in the journal Psychological Science.

#65784. Rainforest ferns from an ancient lineage have a surprisingly young family tree

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (904 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Rainforest ferns from an ancient lineage have a surprisingly young family tree

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An ancient lineage of rainforest ferns reveals how rising mountains and retreating wetlands may have shaped plant diversity across tropical America.
  • Some rainforest ferns belong to a lineage that stretches back to the age of dinosaurs.
  • Researchers at the University of Turku and Aarhus University have reconstructed the history of tropical American Danaea ferns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An ancient lineage of rainforest ferns reveals how rising mountains and retreating wetlands may have shaped plant diversity across tropical America.

Some rainforest ferns belong to a lineage that stretches back to the age of dinosaurs. Yet roughly half its living species arose within the past six million years, as mountains rose and landscapes changed.

Researchers at the University of Turku and Aarhus University have reconstructed the history of tropical American Danaea ferns.

The findings draw on decades of work identifying ferns and establishing where they grow. That groundwork made it possible to investigate how the group spread and diversified.

“We have conducted extensive research at the University of Turku in order to understand the biodiversity of the Amazon rainforest,” said senior author Hanna Tuomisto, a professor of ecology.

“In the last 25 years, we have discovered and described 47 new Danaea species previously unknown to science, and have clarified the distribution and phylogenetic relationships of the species in the Danaea genus.”.

“We have now been able to link this information to the geological and climatic history of tropical America.”.

Recent findings suggest that the team combined DNA evidence from 78 species with 2,289 verified records of where the ferns grow. These records helped reconstruct where ancestral ferns probably lived and the elevations they occupied.

The genetic analysis included 11 species that had not yet been formally described.

The researchers’ preferred estimate suggests that the Danaea lineage split from the lineage of its closest living relatives about 128 million years ago, during the Early Cretaceous.

The common ancestor of its surviving species lived much later, around 53 million years ago. The researchers traced that ancestor to Amazonia.

Recent findings suggest that but an ancient lineage need not consist of ancient species. About half of today’s Danaea species originated during the past six million years.

This complicates a familiar explanation for tropical richness: favorable conditions allowed species to accumulate over immense stretches of time.

Persistence mattered, but the landscape also kept changing, creating opportunities for new species.

According to recent reports, fern diversity generally reaches its greatest heights in tropical mountain forests. Danaea follows a different pattern: Amazonia has consistently held its largest pool of species in the reconstruction.

Sources indicate that “Mountain rainforests are home in particular to an abundance of epiphytes – plants that grow on top of other plants. Danaea ferns, on the other hand, grow on the forest floor,” said lead author Venni Keskiniva, a postdoctoral researcher at Turku.

“These research results are, in fact, similar to those obtained for trees, which are also the most species-rich in lowland rainforests.”.

Where a plant lives within a forest may therefore help explain where its group becomes most diverse. Findings from one fern group cannot automatically describe them all.

The Andes still played an key role. Although Amazonia contained more species, the mountains became the leading source of dispersal to other regions.

Industry observers note that mountain formation affected far more than the slopes themselves. As the Andes rose, they changed rainfall patterns along with the soils developing across neighboring lowlands.

According to recent reports, vast wetlands once occupied much of western Amazonia. Their drainage near the end of the Miocene opened additional land for forest plants to colonize.

The resulting western Amazonian soils were generally richer in nutrients and more variable, than soils in central Amazonia.

Those differences may have encouraged plants to specialize in different environments.

The timing fits the fern history. Most new Amazonian species arising within the past six million years appeared in western Amazonia during the last three million.

Industry observers note that new land in southern Central America also offered room for expansion. Arriving lineages frequently gave rise to additional species as the region’s landscapes developed.

The first mountain-adapted Danaea lineages appeared around 20 million years ago, following an intensification of Andean uplift. Several later spread into regions farther from the equator.

Their earlier move uphill may have helped them cope with the conditions they encountered there.

“As the plants had already adapted to the cooler climate of the mountains, it may have been easier for them to spread to areas where the temperature differences between the seasons are greater,” Keskiniva said.

Lineages that remained adapted to Amazonian lowlands tended to stay within that region.

The repeated sequence of mountain colonization followed by expansion suggests that climate tolerance influenced which routes were available.

According to recent reports, the mountains could both separate populations and help others reach upcoming habitats. Their role changed as the landscape rose and different fern lineages established themselves.

Assigning dates to this history was difficult. Many relevant fossils are fragmentary, and researchers disagree about where they belong in the family tree.

In a recent development, the team compared three dating approaches, which produced substantially different ages. It favored the reconstruction most consistent with other biological and geological evidence.

Recent findings suggest that the dates remain estimates, and coinciding events do not establish a cause by themselves. Still, the findings connect the survival of ancient lineages with much younger episodes of diversification.

“The biodiversity in rainforests is the result of a long history, but its formation has also been greatly influenced by events that are relatively recent on a geological time scale,” Keskiniva concluded.

The study is published in the journal Frontiers of Biogeography.

#65782. Industry News: Cattails send oxygen into marsh mud, where it can change the soil chemistry

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1398 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Cattails send oxygen into marsh mud, where it can change the soil chemistry

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that cattails grow in mud with almost no oxygen, but their roots bring some in.
  • The roots of cattails can grow in oxygen-poor marsh mud.
  • Part of that oxygen then escapes into the surrounding mud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that cattails grow in mud with almost no oxygen, but their roots bring some in. A fresh study found that growing roots release oxygen even at night.

The roots of cattails can grow in oxygen-poor marsh mud. To keep these roots alive, the plant carries air down from its leaves.

Part of that oxygen then escapes into the surrounding mud.

Industry observers note that it has generally been assumed that this leak occurs mostly in daylight. During the day, the leaves produce oxygen and their pores stay open to the air.

A laboratory study of narrowleaf cattails has found that daylight altered the leak only slightly. Instead, oxygen appeared wherever a new root or underground stem was growing. It remained there through the night as well.

The findings suggest that the season of root growth may matter more for marsh chemistry than the time of day.

The study was conducted by Ilana Stein and Zoe Cardon of the Ecosystems Center. This center is part of the Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL) in Woods Hole, Massachusetts.

In a recent development, four plants were examined one at a time in boxes of marsh mud. No measurements were made in a marsh itself.

Recent findings suggest that flooding leaves the soil of a wetland without oxygen. Most wetland plants cope with this through spongy tissue in their leaves, stems and roots that is filled with air.

This tissue serves as a kind of snorkel for the plant. Oxygen travels through it from the air above the water to the root tips below.

Narrowleaf cattail is particularly well adapted to flooded ground. Air spaces were found by earlier studies to make up as much as 74% of its leaf tissue.

In the roots, the figure reached as much as 32%.

Some of the oxygen that arrives is used by the roots and the rest can leak away. This leaked oxygen allows microbes that depend on it to survive in mud where they otherwise could not.

It has been revealed that certain microbes consume methane before the gas can enter the plant and escape through its leaves. Others break down organic matter in the mud and could reduce how much carbon the soil stores.

The same leak is also valuable to people. Cattails are planted in constructed wetlands that treat wastewater and are used to clean up contaminated soil. Both of these uses rely on the oxygen released by their roots.

Industry observers note that cattails and mud were collected by Stein and Cardon from a marsh along the Parker River in northeastern Massachusetts. This marsh forms part of the Plum Island Ecosystems Long Term Ecological Research program.

Each plant was placed in a narrow clear plastic box filled with live mud from the same marsh. The box measured about 15.5 inches tall and 8 inches wide (39 by 20 centimeters).

Much of one inside wall was covered with a film containing a dye that responds to oxygen. A camera photographed the film under blue light.

The colors in every image indicated how much oxygen was present in the mud behind the film.

These films were made by hand by Suzanne Thomas, who works as a senior research assistant at MBL.

Images were captured every few minutes over periods that usually lasted two to three days.

In a recent development, the box itself remained in darkness behind black cloth. Meanwhile, the leaves grew outside under a lamp that was switched on from 5 a.m. to 7 p.m.

According to recent reports, A sensor attached to one leaf collected readings once every minute. It recorded how swiftly the leaf absorbed carbon dioxide and how widely its pores had opened.

The team could therefore compare the activity of the leaves with the oxygen in the mud.

Mud that held no roots also held no oxygen. This changed as soon as part of a cattail grew into it.

Cattails spread by means of horizontal underground stems known as rhizomes. Fresh roots then emerge from these stems.

Whenever a new rhizome or root entered a patch of mud, the oxygen level there rose rapidly from zero. It climbed to between 25% and 35% of the amount found in water that is fully saturated with air.

It has been revealed that this oxygen did not persist for long. Around a rhizome, it disappeared after about three days on average. Around a main root, it lasted about four days.

According to the authors, a seal may be partly responsible. Older sections of a cattail root develop a barrier that is thought to keep oxygen inside. This would allow more of it to reach the growing tip.

Stein and Cardon wrote that this barrier and the steady demand for oxygen in the mud may explain the decline.

Industry observers note that in many cases, oxygen returned to the mud a second time. Fine side roots broke through the sealed surface of a main root and oxygen spread through the mud around them.

These later pools of oxygen persisted for about three weeks on average. In one plant, they lasted longer than five weeks.

An earlier study had found that cattail side roots do not develop the barrier that seals a main root.

Sources indicate that as a result, a single root released oxygen into the mud on two occasions. The first release lasted a few days near the tip and the second continued for weeks along the sides.

It has been revealed that earlier studies of rice and a salt marsh cordgrass had reported strong control of the leak by day and night. In the cattails, light did have some effect and this was mostly seen around the side roots.

Across three plants, the gap between the highest and lowest oxygen levels of each day averaged about 3% of saturation. No daily pattern could be detected in the fourth plant.

New growth therefore changed oxygen levels far more than the cycle of day and night.

Industry observers note that the oxygen in the mud also did not follow the activity of the leaves. It increased during the first two to three hours of light. For the rest of the day, it declined even though the leaves were becoming more active.

Industry observers note that after the lights were turned off, the oxygen fell for about two hours. It then rose slowly until the following morning.

Mud consumes oxygen swiftly on its own. Oxygen-rich water was injected into mud that held no roots. The oxygen was gone within about an hour and a half.

The roots must therefore have continued to release oxygen in the dark.

The authors wrote that it remains unclear how cattails achieve this without exhausting the oxygen in their own air spaces.

One explanation they proposed is that the leaf pores did not close completely at night. Air could then have continued to enter the plant.

Methane, soil carbon, and microbes were not examined in the study.

The study also followed just four plants of a single species. None of them was kept in its box for more than two months.

If growth is what controls the oxygen, then the next question is when cattails grow underground.

Stein is a postdoctoral researcher in Cardon’s lab. She said the results turned the team’s attention to the timing of root growth across the year.

Recent findings suggest that earlier field data and models suggest that cattail rhizomes gain the most mass in mid to late summer. This follows the expansion of the leaves.

The authors wrote that oxygen from fresh rhizomes and their roots may be especially intense during that period.

Methane is released by wetlands naturally and oxygen around roots can reduce it.

“Natural greenhouse gas emissions have been happening forever,” noted Cardon, a senior scientist at MBL.

She noted the team hopes to identify natural processes that could act as levers on those emissions.

Industry observers note that the cattails were not followed through a complete growing season or observed in a marsh. The authors wrote that understanding when rhizomes and roots grow through the year should become a priority.

In their view, such knowledge is needed to understand the chemistry of marshes where cattails dominate.

The full study was published in the journal New Phytologist.

#65781. Some patients who appear unresponsive can control a computer with their thoughts

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1070 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Some patients who appear unresponsive can control a computer with their thoughts

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One in three ICU patients who appeared comatose changed a beeping tone by thinking, and that sign of hidden consciousness predicted recovery.
  • Recent findings suggest that after a severe brain injury, a patient may show no visible response when doctors ask them to move.
  • In a New York intensive care unit, 13 of 41 patients who appeared unresponsive changed how fast a sound beeped by trying to open and close a hand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One in three ICU patients who appeared comatose changed a beeping tone by thinking, and that sign of hidden consciousness predicted recovery.

Recent findings suggest that after a severe brain injury, a patient may show no visible response when doctors ask them to move. But their brain waves can sometimes reveal that they’re following the command.

In a New York intensive care unit, 13 of 41 patients who appeared unresponsive changed how fast a sound beeped by trying to open and close a hand.

In a recent development, electrodes on the scalp recorded the patients’ brain waves. A bedside computer detected signals linked to the attempted movement and adjusted the beeping the patients heard through headphones.

The 13 who could do it were also far more likely to regain consciousness by hospital discharge.

A year later, they were far more likely to be able to look after themselves for hours at a time.

Jan Claassen, a professor of neurology at Columbia University’s Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons, led the study.

He also runs the neurocritical care unit at NewYork-Presbyterian and Columbia University Irving Medical Center, where the patients were treated.

According to recent reports, in a 2019 study, his team recorded brain waves while unresponsive patients were told to open and close a hand. A computer program found that about 15% of them were trying to comply.

Recent findings suggest that some patients showed brain activity consistent with following a command even though they did not visibly move. Researchers call this cognitive motor dissociation.

“Our brain-computer interface is only a first step, but it demonstrates that, in principle, we could hopefully in the future give some of these patients a voice,” Claassen said.

Most brain-computer interfaces that let paralyzed people type, play games, or move a robotic arm use a chip implanted on the brain, and they need long training.

Neither suits someone who was healthy last week and isn’t responding now.

So the team used the 21 EEG electrodes already glued to each patient’s scalp.

Through headphones, a recorded voice mentioned “to make the beep sound faster, keep opening and closing your right hand,” then “to make the beep sound slower, stop opening and closing your right hand.”.

A bedside computer read the brain waves as they came in and changed the beeps when it detected the effort.

Each session was two five-minute practice rounds, during which the program learned that patient’s signals, and then a ten-minute test with no help.

The voice encouraged patients when the beeps changed and congratulated them when they hit the target.

The 41 patients were tested a median of five days after their injuries. Their median age was 65, and most had suffered a stroke, a brain bleed, a cardiac arrest, or a head injury.

According to recent reports, thirteen of the 41 patients, or 32%, passed the test on at least one try. Six of them did it within the first week after their injury, which surprised the researchers.

Recent findings suggest that for comparison, all eight healthy volunteers controlled the tone, and so did nine of 22 conscious patients in the same unit. The conscious patients who failed were mostly sedated, agitated, or unable to speak after a stroke.

It has been revealed that the unresponsive patients who succeeded were slow. Their brain signals revealed up about 50 seconds after each instruction.

Conscious patients took about 17 seconds and healthy volunteers about 15. A patient who looks like they are ignoring a command may simply be answering it late.

In a recent development, each patient also took the team’s older command-following exam, the one from 2019. Eight of the 41 passed it. Every one of those who was tested on the tone the same day could control it.

But nine of the 33 patients who failed the older exam could control the tone anyway.

The authors wrote that the beeping feedback may simply be more engaging than a voice repeating the same command.

“EEG is used in clinical practice every day in the ICU,” Claassen stated.

“The only sophisticated part is the computer program we wrote, which analyzes the data in real time and modulates the feedback to the patient.”.

Four of the 13 patients who controlled the tone regained consciousness before leaving the hospital.

Among the 28 patients who could not control the beeping, only one had regained consciousness by hospital discharge.

A year later, six of the 13, or 46%, could be left alone for at least eight hours a day without help. Two of the 28 others, or 7%, could. Patients who had failed both tests did worst of all.

Industry observers note that of those 24 patients, not one recovered that much. By then 17 of the 41 had died, 14 of them after life support was withdrawn.

The deaths after withdrawal are why the authors wrote at length about ethics.

In a recent development, four of the 13 patients who controlled the tone died after life support was withdrawn. The authors cautioned that a negative result cannot rule out awareness.

The study covered one hospital and 41 patients with very different injuries, some of them sedated during testing.

According to recent reports, patients who recovered were also examined more often, which could have made recovery easier to spot in them. The authors wrote that the result needs repeating at other centers before it guides care.

It has been revealed that controlling a tone is also not talking. The study didn’t try to get a yes or a no from anyone. The authors wrote that doing so may need a level of awareness beyond what this test detects.

Families and the conscious patients were asked what they wanted.

All 37 who answered supported the idea, and they asked for a loved one’s voice in place of the recording, and for ways to signal pain, hunger, or simple awareness.

“Our goal is to refine the system so that patients can tell their doctors and loved ones how they are feeling – if they are in pain or hungry, for instance – with more direct communication,” Claassen remarked.

For some patients who showed no visible response at the bedside, the beeps offered evidence that they could follow a command.

The full study was published in the journal Brain.

#65779. Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1276 w)
📖 Baca

Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.
  • Industry observers note that meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group.
  • In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.

Industry observers note that meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group. How well can one find its way alone?

In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.

Industry observers note that after release, 18 reached a familiar spot or found their group. Fourteen headed first to the burrow where the group had slept.

The team found no clear advantage for older or more experienced animals.

The researchers suggest that daily group travel may give meerkats enough experience to navigate alone.

The study was led by Mathilde Martin of the University of Zurich. The team worked alongside the Kalahari Meerkat Project, which follows about 15 wild groups accustomed to people.

The project is run from the Kalahari Research Centre, which is known as the KRC.

“At the KRC, our work with meerkats allows us to distract them with a water bottle and fit their collar in a few seconds while they stand upright drinking; a mere formality for them,” Martin said.

It has been revealed that A GPS tag on each collar logged the position of the animal once every second. A radio transmitter was also fitted, along with a small audio recorder for the meerkat’s calls.

Sources indicate that the team tested a total of 20 adults from five groups between January and March 2025. Fifteen of these animals were male, whereas only five of them were female.

Each meerkat was caught while its group was foraging and was released up to 0.9 miles (1.5 kilometers) away.

Such a distance is greater than the ground usually covered by a meerkat group in a whole day.

The release sites were located inside the territory of each group. The team chose areas that the group had not visited for at least 30 days.

Homing experiments of this kind have previously been carried out on honeybees and desert ants. Highly social animals that travel in tight groups have rarely been tested in the same way.

This is because the knowledge of one animal is difficult to separate from the decisions of the group.

According to recent reports, eighteen of the 20 meerkats left the release site. The sleeping burrow, the capture spot or the group itself was reached by all 18 of them.

Some of the meerkats departed almost at once, whereas others circled the release site for nearly 90 minutes.

The area covered by them ranged from half an acre to almost 17 acres (2,050 to 68,200 square meters).

A meerkat rarely strayed from its course once a direction had been chosen. Sixteen of the animals aimed for a fixed place.

The sleeping burrow was visited first by 14 of those 16.

On average, the straight-line distance to the target amounted to 82% of the distance actually walked by the meerkat.

Sources indicate that the release areas had not been visited by the group for a month. The team therefore concluded that the meerkats had been navigating from long-term memory.

Two males never left the release site, and they were carried back to their groups after 90 minutes. They were no younger or less experienced than the others.

The authors suspect that stress kept them there, and not a lack of knowledge.

Some meerkats had been expected to navigate better than others. Subordinate males sometimes leave the group and go alone in search of mates.

Other females are occasionally driven out for a while by the dominant female.

Industry observers note that solo trips of this kind could be counted as practice. The researchers also considered the age of each animal, together with the time it spent on guard duty.

Attention was given as well to how often it scent-marked the territory or dug at shelters.

None of those traits predicted how long a meerkat explored. Neither did they predict how accurately it set off or how straight it travelled.

No clear difference was found between males and females either, although only five females took part.

The authors think that the explanation lies in the territory itself. It is small and stable, with 0.3 to 0.6 miles (0.5 to 1 kilometer) covered by a group daily.

The whole territory has probably been crossed several times by each member by the time adulthood is reached.

The authors wrote that pigeons of different ages are likewise able to find their way home equally well.

Sources indicate that on the way home, the meerkats spent about two-thirds of their time searching for cues. Most of the remaining time was spent moving.

Few of them stopped to eat, and those that did only grabbed millipedes crawling on the sand.

According to recent reports, the animals stood upright or climbed a bush or tree trunk in order to scan the landscape. Overall, they spent 10 times longer on looking than on sniffing.

This balance between looking and sniffing was altered late in the trip. By that stage, a meerkat had reached its target and was searching for its group. Sniffing then took up more than 20% of its cue-searching time.

Along the way, meerkats were often seen sniffing around boltholes. These are the small shelters that the animals dig across their territory. An earlier experiment had found that meerkats remember where their boltholes are.

The authors suggested that boltholes may serve as landmarks in a meerkat’s memory of its territory.

The search was not ended by reaching the burrow, because the group could have moved on since the capture.

Sources indicate that thirteen of the 20 meerkats rejoined their groups on their own. The slowest took almost three hours.

The burrow or the capture site was reached by five others. The group had nevertheless not been found by them when the three-hour limit ran out.

These animals were caught again and returned by the team.

It has been revealed that the researchers could not explain why some meerkats succeeded while others did not. Success was not predicted by a straighter trip to the burrow.

Nor was it predicted by the number of scent marks left behind by the group.

Sources indicate that the tracking of a group was compared by the authors to a predator following its prey. The target keeps moving and its route is not known to the searcher.

Recent findings suggest that twenty animals make up a small sample, as the authors wrote. All of them were subordinate adults older than 10 months, so pups and dominant animals were not tested.

Recent findings suggest that every release was also made inside familiar territory. The results therefore do not show how a meerkat would manage in a place it does not know.

Sources indicate that two reasons for looking around could not be fully separated either. A lone meerkat that scans the landscape may be checking for predators as much as searching for landmarks.

If many group members know the territory, the next question is who leads when the group moves.

The authors want to know whether certain traits influence which animal takes the lead. The physical needs of an animal and its social rank are two examples.

Co-author Benjamin Robira mentioned the team now wants to understand what makes up a meerkat’s mental picture of its territory.

The researchers also intend to study how the animals get from one point to another.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

The Forever Chemicals Wreaking Havoc on Our Planet Are About to Meet Their Kryptonite

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the most worrisome side effects of modern life is a class of chemicals called per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS.
  • Today, nearly all humans, including newborns, have detectable levels of PFAS in their blood.
  • One promising approach to combating PFAS is to find a way to break their super-strong chemical bonds, then bake that chemistry into next-generation filters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most worrisome side effects of modern life is a class of chemicals called per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS. These man-made compounds show up in everything from non-stick pans to fast-food wrappers. They’re called “forever chemicals” because their carbon-fluorine bonds are so strong that they barely break down. The PFAS family includes nearly 15,000 different compounds, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, but the FDA tests food and animal feed for only a couple dozen of them.

Today, nearly all humans, including newborns, have detectable levels of PFAS in their blood.

One promising approach to combating PFAS is to find a way to break their super-strong chemical bonds, then bake that chemistry into next-generation filters. Right now, filters can trap a variety of PFAS but can’t destroy them, meaning the filters basically just move the toxic chemicals from one place to another. However, a study in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences describes a filter that uses hydrogen to attack carbon-fluorine bonds. When tested against six PFAS of regulatory concern, it worked on all of them.

“PFAS are hard to break down, and normal processes that we use don’t work,” Arizona State University’s Bruce Rittmann, the senior author of the study, said in a press statement. “We showed that this mechanism worked for all six. It’s a universal mechanism.”.

Sources indicate that hydrogen is essential for this process because once activated into a reactive form, it drives a process known as “hydrodefluorination,” stripping and replacing the fluorine and forming carbon-hydrogen bonds. To activate that hydrogen, Rittman and his team used palladium nanoparticles that can convert the hydrogen gas into its much-needed reactive form.

“The palladium attracts the PFAS molecule, and the palladium attracts the hydrogen and puts them together,” Rittmann said in a press statement.

As hydrogen and PFAS travel through the membrane, both are attracted to the palladium catalyst. However, hydrogen isn’t simply added to the waste stream—instead, it’s fed directly into the membrane itself. This gives the filter the perfect opportunity to chemically dismantle those troublesome carbon-fluorine bonds. Over two months of continuous operation, the membrane broke apart most of the PFAS it captured. It removed 90 percent of the chemicals and stripped about 83 percent of their fluorine.

In a recent development, that’s a huge advancement for combating the proliferation of PFAS in the natural environment, but a massive limitation will be cost. Simply put, palladium isn’t cheap, and Rittman estimates that roughly a kilogram of the stuff costs about $50,000. The new approach could be paired with conventional treatments, which would first concentrate the PFAS into a smaller waste stream that the palladium membrane could then destroy.

In a recent development, “Decades of extensive deployment of PFAS in firefighting foams, oil- and water-repellent surfaces, non-stick cookware, and food-contact materials have created diffuse, chronic inputs into watersheds and drinking-water supplies,” the authors wrote in the study. “Hydrogen-driven hydrodefluorination offers a direct reductive route under comparatively mild conditions.”.

Satellites watched a cluster of thunderstorms become Cyclone Xavier

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Satellite images show how promptly Tropical Cyclone Xavier developed a distinct eye as it strengthened near the northern Cook Islands.
  • Today’s Image of the Day features Tropical Cyclone Xavier spinning over the South Pacific near the northern Cook Islands.
  • Bands of white clouds curve around the storm’s eye.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Satellite images show how promptly Tropical Cyclone Xavier developed a distinct eye as it strengthened near the northern Cook Islands.

Today’s Image of the Day features Tropical Cyclone Xavier spinning over the South Pacific near the northern Cook Islands.

Bands of white clouds curve around the storm’s eye. In satellite images from a few hours earlier, the eye was still forming.

The MODIS instrument aboard NASA’s Aqua satellite captured this scene at 4:53 p.m. Cook Islands time on November 16, 2026.

By then, Xavier’s strongest sustained winds were estimated at about 120 miles per hour.

The clouds would tighten around a storm that was still gaining strength.

A few days earlier, the system that became Xavier was a loose cluster of thunderstorms.

In microwave satellite images from November 14, its structure was hard to make out.

By late November 16, distinct rainbands curved around a well-defined eye.

A separate sequence from the GOES-18 weather satellite shows the eye becoming easier to pick out over the course of hours.

The difference between those views comes down to what each instrument can see.

A daylight image like this one shows sunlight reflected by clouds and the ocean.

High clouds can hide the circulation beneath them, making it difficult to tell where a developing storm is centered.

Microwave observations can reveal parts of the rain structure beneath those clouds, giving forecasters another way to follow a storm as it organizes.

The eye is typically the calmest part of a mature tropical cyclone. Air sinks there, which helps keep clouds from forming.

It has been revealed that just outside it, warm, moist air rises in a ring of thunderstorms called the eyewall. That ring is usually where the storm’s strongest winds are found.

Farther from the center, the sweeping bands visible from space can bring bursts of heavy rain and wind, with quieter stretches in between.

Someone on an island can experience several rounds of rough weather as successive bands pass overhead, even when the eye stays out at sea.

Sources indicate that from above, the bands look like parts of a single spiral. On the ground, they can feel like a series of separate storms.

The ocean beneath Xavier was about 84 degrees Fahrenheit, warm enough to supply plenty of heat and moisture. Winds also changed relatively little with height.

That meant there was little wind shear to tilt the storm and push its thunderstorms away from the center, allowing them to build around the same developing circulation.

Xavier also formed near the southwestern edge of a broad stretch of unusually warm water associated with El Niño.

During El Niño years, cyclones in the Southwest Pacific tend to form farther toward the central Pacific, shifting where island communities are most likely to encounter them.

Xavier developed on the eastern side of the international date line, near the northern Cook Islands.

The storm eventually reached Category 5 on the scale used in the South Pacific. As it moved west, it encountered drier air and stronger wind shear and began to weaken.

On Manihiki, one of the northern Cook Islands, the rain kept falling after the winds began to ease.

A resident told Pacific Media Network that some homes had lost sections of corrugated roofing and that electricity remained a concern.

The island was relying on solar power after losing its main diesel generator more than a year earlier, and the storm’s persistent cloud cover made it harder to keep batteries charged.

Emergency generators helped residents keep essential supplies cold. The island had also begun preparing well before Xavier appeared on satellite maps.

Each October, the island council begins removing hazardous coconut trees near homes and roads, a practice shaped by the damage Cyclone Martin inflicted on the northern Cook Islands in 1997.

Aqua passed over Xavier once that afternoon, catching a brief moment when the storm’s eye was in clear view.

On Manihiki, one of the most consequential features of the storm was the cloud cover that lingered after the worst winds had passed.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin, using MODIS data.

💡 Key Takeaways
